issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court must address the material issues raised by the parties and assess the evidence as required when deciding an appeal from a decree.
material_facts: The High Court decided the appeal primarily on the purchaser’s readiness and willingness to perform the contract.
It did not examine other material issues, including whether subsequent purchasers had notice of the agreement.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and restored the trial court’s decree.
issues.conclusion: The High Court failed to consider all material issues as required by Order XLI Rule 31 CPC, and its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 31 CPC requires a first appellate court to state the points for determination, decide them, and give reasons for its decision. The judgment applies this requirement to the High Court’s first appeal under Section 96 CPC.

predicates.first_appeal_from_a_decree: A party brought a first appeal from a trial court decree.
predicates.appellate_court_omitted_material_issues: The appellate court decided only some issues and left other material issues unresolved.

issues.definition: When a first appellate court leaves material issues unresolved, its judgment is inadequate.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance may be found ready and willing where the evidence supports the purchaser’s financial capacity and the alleged abandonment of the contract is not proved.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded that he had always been ready and willing to perform the agreement.
Two witnesses supported his evidence that he had sufficient means to purchase the property.
The seller’s allegation that the purchaser had said she could sell the property to someone else was not established by evidence.
The trial court found the purchaser ready and willing, while the High Court relied on delay and lack of steps to perform to reach the opposite conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s finding that the purchaser was not ready and willing was perverse and contrary to the evidence; the trial court’s finding was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed readiness and willingness from the pleadings and evidence, including evidence of financial capacity and whether the alleged abandonment of the contract was proved. It cited no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this issue.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and purchaser_claimed_readiness_and_willingness and evidence_supported_financial_capacity and alleged_abandonment_was_not_proved

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser sought specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.purchaser_claimed_readiness_and_willingn: The purchaser pleaded that he was ready and willing to perform his contractual obligations.
predicates.evidence_supported_financial_capacity: Witness evidence supported that the purchaser had the means to complete the purchase.
predicates.alleged_abandonment_was_not_proved: The seller’s allegation that the purchaser had given up the contract or permitted a sale to another person was not established by evidence.

issues.definition: A purchaser who sought specific performance, claimed readiness and willingness, had supporting evidence of financial capacity, and was not proved to have abandoned the contract is ready and willing.

issues.legal_issue: A power-of-attorney holder may testify about acts performed by the holder but may not testify in place of the principal about the principal’s personal acts or matters within the principal’s personal knowledge.
material_facts: The seller did not testify in person.
A power-of-attorney holder gave evidence concerning matters including whether the purchaser had said he could not raise the balance of the purchase price.
The purchaser denied making that statement, and the seller’s allegation was not established by evidence.
issues.conclusion: The power-of-attorney holder could not depose for the seller about acts performed by the seller or matters within the seller’s personal knowledge.
issues.legal_principle: Order III Rules 1 and 2 CPC permit a power-of-attorney holder to act for the principal, but the term “acts” does not authorize the holder to testify in place of the principal about the principal’s personal acts or knowledge. The court relied on Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani v. Indusind Bank Ltd., M/S Shankar Finance and Investment v. State of A.P., and Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha.

predicates.civil_case: The matter is a civil proceeding in which a party’s evidence is relevant.
predicates.witness_is_power_of_attorney_holder: The witness is authorized to act for a principal under a power of attorney.
predicates.matter_concerns_principal_personal_acts: The evidence concerns acts done by the principal, or matters within the principal’s personal knowledge, rather than acts done by the witness under the power of attorney.

issues.definition: In a civil case, a power-of-attorney holder cannot testify in place of the principal about the principal’s personal acts or knowledge.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be enforced against subsequent purchasers who had notice of the prior agreement, while land acquired or purchased without notice may be excluded from the relief.
material_facts: The trial court found that purchasers other than one purchaser had notice of the earlier agreement.
The agreement and sale deed contained recitals acknowledging the earlier agreement.
One purchaser was found to have acquired a small portion without notice, and the plaintiff did not seek to disturb that purchaser’s possession.

Part of the suit land had been acquired, and the Supreme Court restored the trial court’s decree for the land that remained available, excluding the acquired land and the portion bought without notice.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to have a sale deed executed for the suit land still available, except the acquired land and the portion purchased without notice.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the trial court’s findings on notice and the contents of the agreement and sale deed in restoring specific-performance relief, while preserving the exclusion for the purchaser without notice. No specific statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser sought specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_had_notice: A later purchaser knew of the earlier agreement to sell.
predicates.contracted_land_remains_available: The relevant contracted land remains available and has not been acquired or transferred to a purchaser protected by lack of notice.

issues.definition: When specific performance is sought, the later purchaser had notice, and the contracted land remains available, specific performance is enforced against that purchaser.

issues.legal_issue: A person who has no title to land has no right to retain compensation paid for its acquisition.
material_facts: The purchaser had not acquired title to the land for which acquisition compensation was paid.
He withdrew the compensation after undertaking to return it if the court so ordered.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser had no right to the compensation and was ordered to refund it to the seller with interest.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that a person who had not acquired title to the land had no right to receive its acquisition compensation, and enforced the undertaking to return the amount. No specific statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.claimant_has_no_title_to_land: The person claiming or retaining compensation has not acquired title to the land for which it was paid.
predicates.claimant_withdrew_compensation_under_und: The person withdrew the compensation after undertaking to return it if ordered by the court.

issues.definition: A person without title who withdrew compensation under an undertaking must refund it.
